extracted.intended_audience: mathematics education researchers and educators studying student reasoning about combinatorial proof
extracted.subtask_description: Frameworks and methodological criteria for describing, eliciting, and coding students' combinatorial-proof activity and beliefs (including task design, interview protocols, and coding using proof-schemes). Relevant to qualitative studies of combinatorial proof in undergraduate settings.

rubrics_metrics.name: Lockwood (2013) model — sets of outcomes
rubrics_metrics.description: Sets of outcomes represent collections of objects that are enumerated, which also encompasses different ways those objects may be represented or 'encoded' (e.g., binary strings, sequences where order does not matter).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Use sets of outcomes as one component when characterizing students' combinatorial thinking or as the enumerated domain in a combinatorial proof; consider different encodings of the same outcome set when constructing bijective arguments.

rubrics_metrics.name: Lockwood (2013) model — counting processes
rubrics_metrics.description: Counting processes describe the mental or physical operations a counter uses to generate or enumerate sets of outcomes (e.g., applying the Multiplication Principle, constructing a case breakdown).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Interpret expressions and student moves as instantiations of counting processes; look for operations such as staged choices (multiplication) or case splits (addition). Example: selecting an unordered committee then choosing a chair suggests a multiplicative process expressed via binomial/factor terms.

rubrics_metrics.name: Lockwood (2013) model — formulas/expressions
rubrics_metrics.description: Formulas/expressions include mathematical expressions whose numerical value(s) are the cardinality of the set of outcomes and are often considered the 'answer' to the counting problem.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Analyze how students map between expressions and the underlying outcomes/processes; expressions can suggest particular counting processes (e.g., n-1 choose k-1 suggests choosing one object then an unordered selection).

rubrics_metrics.name: Lockwood model — bidirectional relationships among components
rubrics_metrics.description: There are bidirectional relationships between sets of outcomes, counting processes, and formulas/expressions: counting processes produce sets of outcomes which correspond to expressions, and given expressions can suggest underlying counting processes or encodings.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Use the bidirectional mapping to diagnose student reasoning: determine whether a student's expression stems from an intended counting process or whether they infer a process from algebraic expressions; this is critical for characterizing combinatorial proofs.

rubrics_metrics.name: Multiplication Principle (MP) as a counting-process standard
rubrics_metrics.description: The Multiplication Principle states that if a procedure can be broken into m successive ordered stages with r1,...,rm outcomes at each stage, independent of prior choices and yielding distinct composite outcomes, then the total number of composite outcomes is r1 × r2 × ... × rm.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Treat MP as a canonical justification for multiplicative counting steps in students' arguments; check independence and distinctness conditions when evaluating whether MP applies.

rubrics_metrics.name: Definition of combinatorial proof (enumerative representation system)
rubrics_metrics.description: Combinatorial proofs are considered enumerative arguments: they explain why an identity holds by counting the same set of outcomes in two ways (situated in an 'enumerative' representation system).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: To qualify an argument as a combinatorial proof in this study, it must directly involve counting (enumerative reasoning) rather than purely algebraic manipulation; evaluate whether both sides are shown to enumerate the same outcome set.

rubrics_metrics.name: Explanatory argument criteria (Lockwood et al., 2020)
rubrics_metrics.description: An argument is explanatory to an individual within a representation system if it 1) begins with axioms/definitions/statements the individual believes, 2) employs inferential schemes that are natural to the individual, and 3) is couched within or mappable to a representation system the individual finds personally valuable.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Use these three conditions to judge whether a combinatorial argument is explanatory for a given reader; recognize that an argument can be explanatory in the enumerative RS but not algebraically explanatory.

rubrics_metrics.name: Engelke & Cadwallader-Olsker grading metric (1–4 scale)
rubrics_metrics.description: Prior study rated students' written combinatorial proofs on a scale from 1 to 4 based on how successful the proofs were and categorized observed student difficulties.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: When assessing written proofs, consider using a multi-point rubric that captures degrees of success and documents common error patterns; note that this study used such a scale to categorize performance (though detailed descriptors are from Engelke & Cadwallader-Olsker).

rubrics_metrics.name: Pseudo-semantic proof production (anti-pattern)
rubrics_metrics.description: Defined as 'the attempt to engage in a semantic proof production process, but relying on the syntax of a previously encountered proof when faced with a term that the student cannot explain' (i.e., using surface/formal features without semantic understanding).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Treat pseudo-semantic reasoning as an indicator of superficial understanding: a student may produce syntactically plausible arguments that lack genuine mapping to outcomes or processes; code and flag such responses during analysis.

rubrics_metrics.name: Contextual and numerical instantiation as scaffolding strategies
rubrics_metrics.description: Contextual instantiation: situating combinatorial thinking in a concrete context (e.g., committees). Numerical instantiation: substituting specific values for variables to write out terms and discern what a summation counts.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Use these instantiations as instructional or elicitation techniques to help students generate combinatorial proofs, especially for summation identities and bijective arguments; these strategies were empirically found to benefit novice provers.

rubrics_metrics.name: Participant selection criteria for interviews
rubrics_metrics.description: Recruit upper-division students who have completed at least one proof-based college course and who demonstrate familiarity with combinations/binomial coefficients and the ability to navigate basic mathematical proofs.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Use selection interviews with counting/proof tasks to ensure participants meet these inclusion criteria before data collection; this ensures participants have baseline proof experience while minimizing prior combinatorics background.

rubrics_metrics.name: Task design and scaffolding mapping (Table 1)
rubrics_metrics.description: Design tasks with explicit intended purposes: e.g., simple enumeration to list outcomes, subset problems to encourage set-oriented perspectives, find-a-bijection tasks to prepare bijective proofs, even/odd subset tasks to scaffold proving identities involving sums, reverse counting to foster constructing problems that yield specified answers.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Map each task to a scaffolding goal and sequence tasks to build toward bijective combinatorial proofs; encourage set-oriented perspectives and ensure familiarity with ordered/unordered selection distinctions.

rubrics_metrics.name: Interview prompt wording and timing (protocol)
rubrics_metrics.description: Initial prompts asked for 'arguments' rather than 'proofs' to avoid influencing participants' beliefs about whether combinatorial arguments count as rigorous proofs; later tasks used the word 'proof'. Hints/prompts were given only after participants had opportunity to reason independently and only when the interviewer perceived an impasse; hints were infrequent.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Phrase prompts to minimize biasing participants' metacognitive judgments; restrict interviewer assistance to preserve spontaneous reasoning while allowing targeted scaffolding when necessary; document prompt timing and content.

rubrics_metrics.name: Six Arguments handout criterion — combinatorial equality by enumeration
rubrics_metrics.description: Combinatorial justification demonstrates equality by showing both sides enumerate the same set of outcomes in a specified representation (e.g., subsets, committees, binary strings).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Evaluate whether a student's combinatorial argument explicitly identifies the outcome set and demonstrates the two counts are of the same set; use multiple representation systems (subsets, committees, binary strings) as canonical contexts.

rubrics_metrics.name: Thematic coding procedure using Harel & Sowder proof schemes
rubrics_metrics.description: Flag episodes where students discuss perceptions of combinatorial proof; transcribe interviews; code episodes using Harel & Sowder's proof schemes (authoritarian, ritual, perceptual empirical, transformational, contextual restrictive, etc.).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Follow thematic analysis (Braun & Clarke): rewatch videos, familiarize, flag key episodes, code, rewatch and re-code flagged episodes, and discuss coding decisions among authors to ensure consistency. Allow multiple proof-scheme codes per episode if warranted.

rubrics_metrics.name: Mapping utterances to proof-scheme codes (coding rules)
rubrics_metrics.description: Operational mapping examples: utterances about logical structure → analytical proof scheme; appeals to authority (e.g., 'instructor wouldn't accept it') → authoritarian; appeals to surface/ritualistic features (length, symbols) → ritual proof scheme; symbolic manipulation without sense-making → symbolic proof scheme.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Use such mapping heuristics when assigning proof-scheme codes; when ambiguous, discuss among coders and allow multiple codes for a single episode. Check video context to disambiguate.

rubrics_metrics.name: Application scope of proof-schemes — comprehension vs production
rubrics_metrics.description: Proof schemes were applied primarily to students' proof comprehension and reflections rather than to their proof production, because production episodes were predominantly transformational-analytical and thus less informative for the study's focus on perceptions.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Choose whether to apply proof-schemes to production or comprehension based on study goals; explicitly justify this choice in analysis when production would trivially map to a single scheme.

rubrics_metrics.name: Reporting guidance for qualitative frequencies
rubrics_metrics.description: Do not report frequencies when participants received unequal exposure to reflection questions (reporting frequencies would be misleading); instead, report occurrences and illustrative examples.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: When interview question counts vary across participants, prefer descriptive exemplars over numerical frequency claims; clarify limitations in generalization.

rubrics_metrics.name: Students' evaluative criteria for what 'feels like' a proof (empirical rubric of learners)
rubrics_metrics.description: Students often judge proofs by ritualistic/surface features: complexity/length, presence of symbolic algebra or induction, formal-looking structure, and use of familiar symbolic manipulations; lack of these features can lead students to doubt whether an argument counts as a rigorous proof.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: When analyzing student acceptance of combinatorial proofs, code for evidence of ritualistic standards (e.g., 'I just inherently doubt that it could be that simple', 'It's just me saying words'); treat these as legitimate criteria students use even if they diverge from formal mathematical standards.
